document_title: Curtin University AI Use in Research
text:
AI tools can enhance research by quickly summarising or refining text, analysing large data sets, crafting and debugging code, communicating research
results and streamlining repetitive tasks. To use them well, researchers need to protect intellectual integrity and authorship, safeguard intellectual
property (including Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property), use data in culturally appropriate ways, and keep human oversight and expert
judgement at the centre of their work. AI tools must never substitute for human critical thinking, expertise and evaluation.
The guidelines apply to all Curtin researchers, including research students in master and doctoral programs. They cover generative AI tools for text,
images, audio, code and data, as well as generative AI-driven support platforms. They should be read alongside Curtin’s Artificial Intelligence Policy and
the policies of publishers, funders and governments relevant to your research.

When students use AI repeatedly and authentically in learning tasks, they build their ability to judge when AI is
useful, evaluate what it produces, and experience what it means to remain accountable for the final work. When
coupled with learning and assessment designs that ask students to explain how and why they used AI, and to clarify
their own contribution to AI-augmented work, AI-integrated learning can nurture academic integrity behaviours by
rewarding transparency, honesty and accountability. Making these behaviours more visible also means educators
are positioned to guide students’ decision-making, provide feedback on their AI use, and assess not only what
students produce, but how responsibly they arrived there.

Assessment Panels
Each School must have an Assessment Panel comprising Teaching Staff from the Course Stage,
and other Staff as determined by the Executive Dean of the School (e.g. Course Coordinator)
and have oversight by the Associate Dean (Teaching and Learning). The Assessment Panel will
have sufficient subject matter expertise relevant to the Course.
Where Student performance is assessed across different locations, Schools, providers or
Courses, the Course Coordinator(s) must be included in the Assessment Panel.
The Assessment Panel is to holistically evaluate a combined selection of evidence in order to
confirm a Student’s progression and completion with reference to the CLOs.
The Assessment Panel may conduct an informal viva with a Student where they deem it
necessary for Student Identity Verification or to verify CLO progress and achievement.
The Assessment Panel will provide each Student with feedback on Assessments, describing
their progression towards achievement of the CLOs and providing advice about how to best
approach their learning throughout the remainder of their Course.
Consistent with a criterion and standards referenced approach, where grades are provided, the
allocation of a grade must reflect the level of Student attainment in relation to Benchmarked
Standards. Any scaling of marks must be justifiable by reference to Benchmarked Standards
and endorsed by the Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Education).
Consensus moderation must be employed by Assessment Panels to ensure reliable judgements
in relation to Benchmarked Standards during all phases of the Assessment cycle.

For all Units, Unit Coordinators must submit proposed results via the University approved
system by the nominated submission deadline. Proposed results must reflect the level of
Student attainment in relation to Benchmarked Standards.
The Assessment Panel will, for each Student, approve a final Grade consistent with Grading
Schema 1 or Grading Schema 2, as set out in the Admission, Enrolment and Academic Progress
Rules.

Appeals
In addition to any review mechanisms set out in these procedures, Students have the right to
appeal in accordance with the Admission, Enrolment and Academic Progress Rules.

Collection
The University will only collect Personal Information:
for lawful purposes and when reasonably necessary for, or related to, the University’s
functions, services or activities; and
from the individual it relates to, unless:
the individual has consented otherwise;
it is required or authorised by an Australian law, a court or tribunal order; or
it is unreasonable or impracticable to do so.

Security 4 and De-identification 5
The University will take a proactive approach to manage Personal Information and Sensitive
Personal Information (including Health Information) by ensuring appropriate safeguards and
protocols are in place, including by:
only collecting and retaining Personal Information that is necessary for its functions and not
retaining information longer than required;
protecting against Information Breach Incidents, including from misuse, interference, loss and
from unauthorised access, modification, and disclosure;
following a ‘privacy by design’ approach for processes and system change initiatives;
where relevant, undertaking a Privacy Impact Assessment to appropriately consider and
manage privacy risks and impact;
aligning accountabilities and responsibilities of Relevant Data Owners in line with the Data
Governance Framework; and
ensuring storage and retention protocols under the Records Management Policy.
The University will take reasonable steps to de-identify or destroy Personal Information about
an individual where the:
University no longer needs the information for any purpose for which the information may be
used or disclosed by the entity under this policy;
information is not contained in a Commonwealth record; and
University is not required by or under an Australian law, a court or tribunal order, to retain the
information.

Access and use of Personal Information within the University will only be by Staff who would
reasonably be expected to have access to such information and who have a need to use it to
carry out the University’s functions and activities.
Automated Decision-Making 7
The University is committed to ensuring transparency, fairness and accountability in all
automated decision-making processes including by:
assessment of the impact of the automated decision-making processes;
regular review to minimise bias and ensure compliance with applicable privacy laws; and
taking reasonable steps to notify individuals of use of automated decision-making processes.
The University, during its functions and activities, may:
use computer programs, including rule-based systems and artificial intelligence or machine
learning technologies; and
use or engage in third-party services that use computer programs, including rule-based
systems and artificial intelligence or machine learning technologies,
to assist or support in the review and decision-making which could significantly affect
individual rights or interests.
Where these decisions relate to eligibility for services, access to benefits, or other outcomes
that may significantly affect an individual, the University will take reasonable steps to notify
individuals of the:
types of Personal Information used;
nature of decisions made; and
human intervention and review controls in place.
Individuals may request human review of decisions that significantly affect them where
automated decision-making has been used.

Governance Services as its Privacy Officer.

compliance with this policy and applicable privacy legislation together with the development,
maintenance and oversight of the University’s privacy management approach, including:
the University’s privacy management practices;
privacy complaints or concerns in line with the Complaints Policy;

Management Framework to enable ECU to make informed risk-based decisions;
Privacy Impact Assessments with University stakeholders and wider University community as
necessary; and
investigation and response to Information Breach Incident reports (in line with Critical Incident
and Business Continuity Management Policy and supporting procedures and other operational
documents).

text:
The University reserves the right to decide who will and will not be provided access to
University Information Systems and to remove access should the University deem access to no
longer be required or to no longer be in the University’s best interests.

accept accounts on the understanding they are for the exclusive use of the Authorised User
and must not be shared or used by anyone other than the Authorised User.
Passwords, accounts and documented processes required for the access of University
information must be protected and secured in accordance with the conditions under which
access has been provided.

attempt to conceal their identity whilst using University information Systems.
Authorised Users must not acquire, possess, trade, or use hardware or software tools that
could be employed to evaluate or compromise Information Security.
Authorised Users who reasonably suspect the privacy and security of their account has been
compromised must immediately report their concern to the CIO or their nominee.

text:
tasks you intend to use the tool for. Use only fabricated, de-identified, or publicly available
information when testing. This helps protect sensitive data and reduces the risk of copyright
infringement. It's also advisable to test with a topic you're well-versed in so you can assess the
outputs for accuracy and completeness.
Key questions to guide your evaluation
Accuracy: Is the generated response or output accurate and complete? Or does it make
assumptions, misunderstand context, or invent ‘facts’ or citations?
Transparency: does it provide a clear path for how it’s generated its output, such as inline
citations, Boolean search strings, or verifiable sources?
Relevancy: is the generated output relevant to your initial query or topic. For example, are any
source materials directly relevant to the topic and ranked by relevancy, publish date, citation
impact, etc.?
Privacy: Does the developer provide a clear privacy statement explaining how prompts and
user data are collected, stored, and used? Can you configure privacy settings for your account?
If the tool is free, are you confident your data is not being used in exchange for access?
Ethics: Does the developer provide information about how bias is assessed and mitigated? Are
there statements about environmental sustainability, responsible AI practices, or ethical use?
Copyright & Intellectual property: Can you upload content to the tool? If so, how is that content
used? Is it shared beyond your account, retained after use, or used to train future versions of
the AI model?

Tier 2 – AI assistance
If your assessment is assigned Tier 2, you may use AI tools only for the specific
purposes explicitly permitted by your unit coordinator. Don’t assume that AI use

mean ‘general permission to use AI.’

assessment must be your own work, and you remain responsible for all content
submitted, including work that has been shaped or edited using AI tools.

(a) The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is permitted only as an educational/study tool to assist
students in their research and writing to be used in accordance with 6.8(b), and not as a
replacement of their critical thinking and analysis.

ii. there must be a clear indication of where in an assignment AI-generated material is
used;
iii. it is the responsibility of the student to check the accuracy of all information generated
by AI study tools;

academic misconduct referred to in this policy and a penalty or penalties for a proven incident or
incidents of academic misconduct may be imposed in accordance with the relevant penalty matrix.
(d) Unit Coordinators may use AI tools in an assessment within a unit, subject to clearly publishing
the intent and the limitations of the use of such tools within the unit outline.

6.9 Improper use of Artificial Intelligence tools
(a) The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is permitted only as an educational/study tool to assist
students in their research and writing to be used in accordance with 6.8(b), and not as a
replacement of their critical thinking and analysis.
(b) Where any AI-generated outputs are used in assessments;
i. they must be appropriately acknowledged for the submission, including a formal
reference, along with any other sources used;
ii. there must be a clear indication of where in an assignment AI-generated material is
used;
iii. it is the responsibility of the student to check the accuracy of all information generated
by AI study tools;
(c) Improper use of AI-generated outputs in any assessment item/task may lead to the occurrence of
academic misconduct referred to in this policy and a penalty or penalties for a proven incident or
incidents of academic misconduct may be imposed in accordance with the relevant penalty matrix.
(d) Unit Coordinators may use AI tools in an assessment within a unit, subject to clearly publishing
the intent and the limitations of the use of such tools within the unit outline.

• a statement defining expected contributions from each team member may be required to
structure the task to build in individual accountability;
• students may be asked to provide evidence of their individual contributions to the final
product and/or process;
ii. Approach to applying penalty where academic misconduct by an identifiable student (or
students) is proven:
• Award separate marks to each student in the group (guided by action(s) taken in

the contributions of individual students are identified, is not limited to the weighting restrictions
referred to in 5.2(4)(c)(i).
